claim: Mobile genetic elements, or transposons, constitute up to 70% of eukaryotic genomes.
source: Mobile genetic elements, or transposons, constitute up to 70% of eukaryotic genomes (Adams et al., 2000; Britten and Kohne, 1968; Lander et al., 2001; Waterston et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: Transposons are believed to have contributed variation, upon which evolution has acted.
source: and are believed to have contributed variation, upon which evolution has acted (Kazazian, 2004; Levin and Moran, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Transposition introduces non-heritable genetic heterogeneity in somatic cells, including neurons in the brain.
source: Several studies have also suggested that transposition introduces non-heritable genetic heterogeneity in somatic cells, including neurons in the brain (Muotri et al., 2005; Coufal et al., 2009; Baillie et al., 2011; Evrony et al., 2012; Kazazian, 2011; Perrat et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies

claim: Somatic transposition has been implicated in age-dependent neural and cognitive decline.
source: Somatic transposition has been implicated in age-dependent neural and cognitive decline (Bundo et al., 2014; Krug et al., 2017; Li et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Somatic transposition has been implicated in tumorigenesis in other tissues.
source: and tumorigenesis in other tissues (Shukla et al., 2013; Solyom and Kazazian, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: The prevalence of rare somatic transposition is debated due to difficulties in mapping genuine events using whole-genome DNA sequencing.
source: However, the prevalence of rare somatic transposition is debated due to difficulties in mapping genuine events using whole-genome DNA sequencing (Baillie et al., 2011; Evrony et al., 2012, Evrony et al., 2016; Upton et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research discussing methodological challenges

claim: Transposons are expressed and mobile in the brains of Drosophila melanogaster fruit flies.
source: Prior work has suggested that transposons are expressed and mobile in the brains of Drosophila melanogaster fruit flies, and in particular in clonally related sub-populations of mushroom body neurons, called αβ-Kenyon Cells (αβ-KCs) (Li et al., 2013; Perrat et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work

claim: Each fly has ~1800 αβ-KCs.
source: Since each fly has ~1800 αβ-KCs (Aso et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: The αβ-KCs have a defined role in the retrieval of consolidated memory.
source: Moreover, the αβ-KCs have a defined role in the retrieval of consolidated memory (Krashes and Waddell, 2008; Krashes et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: The authors developed a method to extract and sequence gDNA with high genome-wide coverage from most of the ~1800 αβ-KCs from an individual fly.
source: We developed a method to extract and sequence gDNA with high genome-wide coverage from most of the ~1800 αβ-KCs from an individual fly, and from cells taken from the rest of the brain of the same fly.
evidence: Describes the experimental approach developed in this study

claim: Transposon sequences did not accumulate with age.
source: Transposon sequences did not accumulate with age.
evidence: Conclusion from the experimental data presented in the study

claim: Some transposons are more highly expressed in αβ-KCs when compared to the rest of the brain.
source: In addition, although we found some transposons are more highly expressed in αβ-KCs, when compared to the rest of the brain
evidence: Based on experimental measurements in this study

claim: Upregulation of transposons in αβ-KCs did not lead to a measurably larger number of putative insertions in αβ-KC gDNA.
source: their upregulation did not lead to a measurably larger number of putative insertions in αβ-KC gDNA
evidence: Based on experimental data analysis in this study

claim: WGS data contain unexpected sequences indicative of exon translocations.
source: Reanalysis with a novel simulated set of 'immobile genetic elements', rather than transposons, revealed that our Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) data and that from other published work (Khurana et al., 2011) contain unexpected sequences indicative of exon translocations.
evidence: Based on reanalysis of data using a novel approach

claim: The majority of putative de novo transposon insertions result from chimeric artefacts formed during WGS library preparation.
source: A new analysis pipeline that retrieves the precise nucleotide sequence around potential DNA breakpoints revealed that these translocations and the majority of putative de novo transposon insertions result from chimeric artefacts formed during WGS library preparation.
evidence: Based on data from a new analysis pipeline developed in this study

claim: Chimera are prevalent in WGS data prepared from a eukaryote.
source: we here provide evidence that chimera are prevalent in WGS data prepared from a eukaryote
evidence: Based on experimental evidence presented in this study

claim: Somatic transposition is less prevalent in Drosophila than previously envisaged.
source: We conclude that somatic transposition is less prevalent in Drosophila than previously envisaged.
evidence: Main conclusion of the study based on experimental data

claim: mCherry is upregulated by approximately 1000-fold in the purified αβ-KCs.
source: This analysis showed that mCherry is upregulated by approximately 1000-fold in the purified αβ-KCs (Figure 1d).
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 1d

claim: FasII was upregulated by 5-fold in αβ-KCs.
source: As expected FasII was upregulated by 5-fold in αβ-KCs.
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR measurements in this study

claim: The FACS approach efficiently separates labeled αβ-KCs from the rest of the cells in the brain.
source: Our FACS approach therefore efficiently separates labeled αβ-KCs from the rest of the cells in the brain.
evidence: Conclusion based on mCherry and FasII expression data

claim: Pooling gDNA from multiple flies lacks the power to reliably detect rare somatic insertion events at the sequencing depths that can currently be achieved.
source: However, the approach of pooling gDNA from multiple flies lacks the power to reliably detect rare somatic insertion events at the sequencing depths that can currently be achieved.
evidence: Based on theoretical calculation and reasoning about detection limits

claim: At a sequencing depth of 25x with groups of 30 flies, only 1 in 4320 events that occurred in one locus of one cell can be detected.
source: At a sequencing depth of 25x, in theory only 1 in 4320 events that occurred in one locus of one cell can be detected.
evidence: Based on theoretical calculation

claim: Sequencing data obtained from each individual fly exhibited an even distribution of reads across the fly genome.
source: Sequencing data obtained from each individual fly was aligned to the Drosophila reference genome and all samples exhibited an even distribution of reads across the fly genome (Figure 2a).
evidence: Based on sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 2a

claim: 163 new transposon insertions are present in MB008b-GAL4; UAS-mCherry flies but absent in the reference genome.
source: Using this analysis we identified 163 new transposon insertions that are present in our MB008b-GAL4GAL4; UAS-mCherry flies but that are absent in the reference genome.
evidence: Based on TEMP analysis of sequencing data

claim: The 163 insertions represent germline insertions that are unique to the fly strain and have not been mapped before.
source: Importantly, these same 163 insertions were common to all 12 samples prepared from six individual flies demonstrating that they represent germline insertions that are unique to our fly strain and that they have not been mapped before (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on presence of insertions in all samples from all flies

claim: TEMP revealed on average 10,881 putative αβ-KCs specific transposition events per fly.
source: TEMP also revealed on average 10,881 putative αβ-KCs specific transposition events per fly (N = 6, SD = 1960, see Table 1)
evidence: Based on TEMP analysis of sequencing data from 6 flies

claim: A similar number of apparent insertions were found exclusively in the other brain cells and not in αβ-KCs from the same animal.
source: A similar number of apparent insertions were found exclusively in the other brain cells and not in αβ-KCs from the same animal.
evidence: Based on TEMP analysis of sequencing data

claim: Putative de novo somatic insertions appeared to cluster approximately 10 kb up- and down-stream of pre-existing germline locations of transposons.
source: Surprisingly, the positions of these hits revealed a recurring and very particular pattern where putative de novo somatic insertions appeared to cluster approximately 10 kb up- and down-stream of pre-existing germline locations of transposons, a phenomenon that we termed 'hovering' (Figure 2b).
evidence: Based on analysis of TEMP results shown in Figure 2b

claim: The total number of putative somatic insertions was similar in αβ-KCs and in the other brain cells.
source: Finding that the total number of putative somatic insertions was similar in αβ-KCs and in the other brain cells (see Table 1)
evidence: Based on data presented in Table 1

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of putative αβ-KC-specific insertions in gDNA samples prepared from young or old flies.
source: We did not find a significant difference in the number of putative αβ-KC-specific insertions in gDNA samples prepared from young or old flies (Figure 3a).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3a

claim: No significant difference in the number of reads for each known transposon was apparent between gDNA from young and old flies.
source: Again, no significant difference was apparent (Figure 3b,c).
evidence: Based on analysis of sequencing read counts shown in Figures 3b and 3c

claim: The LTR Tabor and LINE-like Ivk were upregulated by approximately 3-fold in αβ-KCs.
source: The LTR Tabor and LINE-like Ivk were upregulated by approximately 3-fold in αβ-KCs
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR measurements

claim: The LTR retrotransposons Gypsy and Blood and the LINE-like Doc3 were expressed at similar levels throughout the brain.
source: whereas the LTR retrotransposons Gypsy and Blood and the LINE-like Doc3 were expressed at similar levels throughout the brain (Figure 3d)
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 3d

claim: No significant correlation was apparent between transposon expression levels and the number of putative αβ-KC somatic insertions.
source: We next plotted these expression levels against the respective number of putative αβ-KC somatic insertions. No significant correlation was apparent
evidence: Based on comparison of expression data with insertion counts

claim: The number of transposon nucleotides in the reference genome and the number of putative insertions of each transposon type in αβ-KC sample gDNA were highly correlated.
source: A comparison between the number of transposon nucleotides in the reference genome and the number of putative insertions of each transposon type in our αβ-KC sample gDNA revealed that these two values were highly correlated (Spearman test, p<0.0001) (Figure 3e).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3e

claim: The average number of detected putative new insertions for each transposon correlates approximately 1:1 with its abundance in the genome.
source: The slope of the fitted line was close to 1 (k = 0.9194 ± 0.04542), suggesting that the average number of detected putative new insertions for each transposon correlates approximately 1:1 with its abundance in the genome.
evidence: Based on linear regression analysis of data

claim: The correlation between insertion frequency and genome abundance is consistent with a scenario where the majority of identified putative de novo insertions result from random sampling of stretches of sequences across the Drosophila genome.
source: This correlation is consistent with a scenario where the majority of identified putative de novo insertions actually result from random sampling of stretches of sequences across the Drosophila genome
evidence: Interpretation of the correlation data

claim: TEMP detected many read-pairs in all WGS samples that qualified as evidence for new IGE insertions.
source: Our analyses detected many read-pairs in all of our WGS samples that qualified as evidence for new IGE insertions (Table 1).
evidence: Based on TEMP analysis using IGEs

claim: The average frequency of IGE insertions in αβ-KCs was 1034.
source: The average frequency of these IGE insertions in αβ-KCs was 1034 (SD = 229.5, N = 6)
evidence: Based on TEMP analysis of IGE insertions

claim: When corrected for the lower copy numbers of IGEs, the frequency of IGE insertions is comparable to that of putative transposon mobilizations detected by TEMP.
source: However, when corrected for the lower copy numbers of IGEs (~30 fold), this value is comparable to that of putative transposon mobilizations detected by TEMP.
evidence: Based on comparison of normalized IGE and transposon insertion frequencies

claim: Apparent IGE mobilizations exhibited a similar hovering pattern around their original locations, as observed for transposons around their respective germline positions.
source: It is also striking that apparent IGE mobilizations exhibited a similar hovering pattern around their original locations, as observed for transposons around their respective germline positions, suggesting this phenomenon is also artificial (Figure 4a).
evidence: Based on analysis of IGE insertion patterns shown in Figure 4a

claim: The number of IGE 'mobilizations' was highest in oocytes of 21 day old dysgenic flies, when compared to oocytes of 4 day old flies, and lowest in the sample taken from flies that were backcrossed to the parental strain.
source: most strikingly, the number of IGE 'mobilizations' was highest in oocytes of 21 day old dysgenic flies, when compared to oocytes of 4 day old flies, and lowest in the sample taken from flies that were backcrossed to the parental strain.
evidence: Based on IGE analysis of published data from Khurana et al., 2011

claim: The different levels of artefacts in each sample follow the apparent observed differences in resident transposon mobilization.
source: The different levels of artefacts in each sample therefore follow the apparent observed differences in resident transposon mobilization.
evidence: Based on comparison of IGE and transposon insertion patterns

claim: There is a strong correlation between the number of putative transposon insertions identified in the oocyte samples and the abundance of each transposon type in the Drosophila genome.
source: Lastly, similar to our observations with our new αβ-KCs data, there is a strong correlation between the number of putative transposon insertions identified in the oocyte samples and the abundance of each transposon type in the Drosophila genome, regardless of whether they are actively expressed or truncated and hence dysfunctional (Spearman test, p<0.0001) (Kaminker et al., 2002) (Figure 4d).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of data from Khurana et al., 2011 shown in Figure 4d

claim: On average, merged contigs were 270 basepairs long.
source: On average, these contigs were actually 270 basepairs long (Figure 5a).
evidence: Based on analysis of merged read pairs shown in Figure 5a

claim: Approximately 4% of read pairs mapped further apart than the expected 250 nucleotides when aligned to the reference genome.
source: To our surprise ~4% of these read pairs mapped further apart than the expected 250 nucleotides when they were aligned to the reference genome (Figure 5b).
evidence: Based on alignment analysis shown in Figure 5b

claim: Breakpoints were evenly distributed throughout the length of all types of transposons.
source: This analysis revealed that breakpoints were evenly distributed throughout the length of all types of transposons (Figure 5c).
evidence: Based on analysis of breakpoint positions shown in Figure 5c

claim: A lack of preference for breakpoints to occur at transposon ends is more compatible with the occurrence of sequence artefacts than genuine transposon insertions.
source: A lack of preference for breakpoints to occur at transposon ends is more compatible with the occurrence of sequence artefacts than genuine transposon insertions.
evidence: Interpretation based on the breakpoint distribution data

claim: The distribution of the size of complementary sequences in chimera from MRTemp sequencing data was remarkably similar to that observed in bacterial DNA.
source: When we plotted the lengths of complementary sequences in chimera from our MRTemp sequencing data, we observed a remarkably similar distribution (Figure 5d).
evidence: Based on comparison of complementary sequence length distributions shown in Figure 5d

claim: Most chimera occurred between fragments that are less than 10,000 nucleotides apart.
source: Most chimera occured between fragments that are less than 10,000 nucleotides apart.
evidence: Based on analysis of fragment size distribution from MRTemp data

claim: The local accumulation, or hovering, of putative transposon (and IGE) insertions around germline locations occurred across a similar range of distances as chimera formation.
source: Strikingly, our previously observed local accumulation, or hovering, of putative transposon (and IGE) insertions around germline locations, occurred across a similar range of distances
evidence: Based on comparison of hovering distances with chimera formation distances

claim: In vitro DNA amplification chimera account for the majority of observed transposon mobilizations.
source: suggesting that in vitro DNA amplification chimera account for the majority of observed transposon mobilizations (Figure 5e)
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including hovering patterns and chimera formation

claim: It is inherently impossible, with TEMP and most other currently used transposon detection methods, to distinguish genuine somatic transposon insertions from chimeric DNA fragments formed during gDNA amplification.
source: Therefore, it is inherently impossible, with TEMP and most other currently used transposon detection methods, to distinguish genuine somatic transposon insertions that occurred in a cell from chimeric DNA fragments that were formed during the amplification of gDNA.
evidence: Conclusion based on the range of chimera formation distances

claim: Some transposon-derived mRNAs are relatively more abundant in αβ-KCs of adult Drosophila than in other brain cells.
source: In the current study, we again find some transposon-derived mRNAs are relatively more abundant in αβ-KCs of adult Drosophila than in other brain cells.
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR measurements in this study

claim: The transposons identified in this study are not the same as those in prior work using a different strain to GFP label αβ-KCs.
source: It is notable that the transposons we identified in this study are not the same as those in our prior work, which used a different strain to GFP label αβ-KCs (Perrat et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on comparison with prior published work

claim: The single fly approach allowed unambiguous identification of germline transposon insertions that are present at low frequencies in a population of flies.
source: The single fly approach in contrast to previous Drosophila studies, allowed us to unambiguously identify germline transposon insertions that are present at low frequencies in a population of flies.
evidence: Based on the ability to detect insertions present in both samples from the same fly but absent in other flies

claim: The fly strain contained many rare germline transposon insertions despite extensive inbreeding.
source: Despite extensive inbreeding, we found that our fly strain contained many rare germline transposon insertions, which were found in both samples from the same fly but were absent in the WGS samples from all other individual flies
evidence: Based on sequencing data analysis

claim: The authors did not detect new transposition events in gDNA from adult fly αβ-KCs beyond the rate of experimental artefacts.
source: Despite the increased transposon expression and the high sensitivity of the mapping approach, we did not detect new transposition events in gDNA from adult fly αβ-KCs beyond the rate of experimental artefacts.
evidence: Main finding of the study based on experimental data

claim: The authors did not find evidence for transposon insertions accumulating in older flies.
source: However, we did not find evidence for transposon insertions accumulating in older flies, even when individual samples were normalized for the estimated rate of chimera formation using our IGE method.
evidence: Based on analysis of data from young and old flies

claim: De novo transposon insertions are not prevalent in αβ-KCs, or other brain cells.
source: Despite identifying experimental artefacts in every data set, our high sequencing coverage, TEMP and MRTemp analyses, suggest that de novo transposon insertions are not prevalent in αβ-KCs, or other brain cells.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple analyses of sequencing data

claim: TEMP analysis suggested that IGEs also mobilize in every gDNA sample prepared from mature neurons.
source: Surprisingly, TEMP analysis suggested that IGEs also mobilize in every gDNA sample prepared from mature neurons
evidence: Based on TEMP analysis using IGEs

claim: WGS data are spoiled by chimeric artefacts that are formed by MDA during sample preparation.
source: These experiments demonstrated that WGS data are spoiled by chimeric artefacts that are formed by MDA during sample preparation.
evidence: Based on MRTemp analysis showing chimera formation

claim: Library artefacts account for the majority of instances that have previously been considered to represent rare somatic transposition events.
source: Since IGE mobilization arises at a similar frequency to that expected of rare somatic transposon insertions, it seems likely that library artefacts account for the majority of instances that have previously been considered to represent rare somatic transposition events.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of IGE and transposon insertion frequencies

claim: DNA chimera are a pervasive issue in Drosophila WGS data.
source: Applying IGE analysis to Drosophila WGS data from another independent study suggests that DNA chimera are a pervasive issue.
evidence: Based on IGE analysis of published data from Khurana et al., 2011

claim: The apparent increase of somatic transposition events between samples in the Khurana et al. study could be explained by an increased abundance of DNA chimera formation.
source: Our IGE analysis of these data revealed that the apparent increase of somatic transposition events between the two samples could also be explained by an increased abundance of DNA chimera formation in the relevant samples.
evidence: Based on IGE analysis of published data

claim: The standard TEMP approach is an unreliable indicator of insertion penetrance.
source: Importantly, since these IGE insertions are simulated, any apparent increase cannot be real which suggests that the standard TEMP approach is an unreliable indicator of insertion penetrance.
evidence: Based on analysis of IGE insertion penetrance

claim: Around 17% of reads that spanned breakpoints contained overlapping palindromic sequences around their breakpoint.
source: We also noted that around 17% of reads that spanned breakpoints contained overlapping palindromic sequences around their breakpoint.
evidence: Based on analysis of MRTemp sequencing data

claim: Palindromic sequences are indicative of chimera formed during gDNA library preparation.
source: Prior work analyzing DNA from Escherichia coli suggested that these palindromic sequences are indicative of chimera formed during gDNA library preparation (Lasken and Stockwell, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on bacterial DNA

claim: The length of palindromic sequences was remarkably similar in fly samples and in Escherichia coli data.
source: Strikingly, the length of these sequences was remarkably similar in our samples and in the Escherichia coli data.
evidence: Based on comparison of complementary sequence length distributions

claim: MDA produces overlapping complementary sequences when preparing gDNA libraries from eukaryotic material.
source: to our knowledge we provide the first experimental evidence that MDA produces overlapping complementary sequences when preparing gDNA libraries from eukaryotic material
evidence: Based on MRTemp analysis of fly DNA

claim: All gDNA sequencing data from flies, rodents, humans and plants, that were prepared using MDA, are subject to the same amplification artefacts.
source: Our findings suggest that all gDNA sequencing data from flies, rodents, humans and plants, that were prepared using MDA, are subject to the same amplification artefacts.
evidence: Inference based on the finding of MDA-induced chimera in fly DNA

claim: Validation of putative de novo insertions using PCR-based approaches on the same material used for WGS is not an adequate test of the putative insertions being genuine.
source: Moreover, since the chimera can be formed at an early stage of the process, the validation of putative de novo insertions using PCR-based approaches on the same material used for WGS is not an adequate test of the putative insertions being genuine (Upton et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference based on understanding of when chimera form during sample preparation

claim: The general IGE approach can be adapted to quantify the abundance of artefactual chimera in gDNA data sets prepared from any organism.
source: Our general IGE approach can be adapted to quantify the abundance of artefactual chimera in gDNA data sets prepared from any organism.
evidence: Based on the demonstrated utility of IGE analysis

claim: An absence of apparent IGE mobilization in sequencing data would indicate a high-fidelity approach and make it possible to identify genuine somatic transposon insertions.
source: An absence of apparent IGE mobilization in sequencing data would indicate a high-fidelity approach and make it possible to identify genuine somatic transposon insertions.
evidence: Logical inference about the utility of IGE analysis for quality control

claim: With current technologies the only convincing evidence for a rare somatic insertion would be breakpoint specific sequence from both ends of a transposon at a specific locus, and sufficiently high sequencing coverage from around the same locus in other tissue from the same individual that shows the insertion is not present.
source: Unfortunately, our analyses lead us to conclude that with current technologies the only convincing evidence for a rare somatic insertion would be breakpoint specific sequence from both ends of a transposon at a specific locus, and in addition, a sufficiently high sequencing coverage from around the same locus in other tissue from the same individual that shows the insertion is not present.
evidence: Conclusion based on the findings about chimera formation
